1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, Queen's Knight Variation
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3.background: Against 2...d5, White can answer 3.cxd5 Nxd5 4.g3 so that Black cannot force a Grünfeld Defence; Mikhail Botvinnik played this line several times in his 1958 world championship match against Vasily Smyslov.
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight towards the centre, where it controls d5 and e4, and keeps e4, g3 and d4 all available. White decides later between taking the centre, a fianchetto set-up and a flexible waiting game, and keeps more options against Black's set-up. The cost is that the centre stays unoccupied for now: Black can contest it at once.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight, watches d4 and e5 and leaves the choice between d4, g3 and Nc3 open until Black's set-up is clear. White can still go for a Queen's pawn game with d4 or for a flexible fianchetto set-up. The move commits little, though it gives Black a free choice of defensive scheme.

1.c4 Nf6 2.d4.strategy: Takes the centre with a pawn, and the game becomes a queen's pawn opening. White gets the c4-d4 pawn pair and extra space, but the pawns become targets, and White must be ready for whichever defence Black picks.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3.strategy: Prepares Bg2, which bears on d5 and along the long diagonal towards b7, and keeps the knights' development and d4 in reserve. White aims for a flexible fianchetto set-up. The cost is that the centre stays unoccupied, and Black can challenge the c4-pawn at once.

1.c4 Nf6 2.e3.strategy: Opens the f1-bishop and supports d4, a solid set-up that commits the e-pawn before Black's set-up is known. It is slow: Black can take space at once and develop freely.

1.c4 Nf6 2.b3.strategy: Prepares Bb2, which bears on e5 and the long diagonal, and supports the c4-pawn. It is sound but slow: the centre stays unoccupied, and Black can claim it with pawns or contest the diagonal.

1.c4 Nf6 2.d3.strategy: Supports a later e4 and opens the c1-bishop. It is sound but modest: d4 would now cost an extra tempo, so Black can take the centre at once and develop freely.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Qc2.strategy: Backs the c4-pawn and prepares e4, but develops no minor piece and leaves the queen where ...Nc6 followed by ...Nb4 can hit it with tempo. Black takes the centre at once while White is still unready.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Qb3.strategy: Eyes b7 and defends the c4-pawn, but the c8-bishop already covers b7 and no minor piece is developed. ...Nc6 followed by ...Na5 then hits the queen and the c4-pawn with tempo, and Black takes the centre while White rearranges.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Qa4.strategy: Brings the queen out before any minor piece and pins the d7-pawn for a moment, but threatens nothing real. ...c6 breaks the pin and prepares ...d5, and Black develops freely while the queen stands on the rim.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Na3.strategy: Defends the c4-pawn and can continue to c2 or b5, but on a3 the knight controls no central square. Black takes the centre in the meantime.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nh3.strategy: Develops the knight on the rim on its way to f4 and leaves the centre alone. Once Black's d-pawn has moved, ...Bxh3 can double White's h-pawns, and f3 was the natural square for the knight.

1.c4 Nf6 2.a3.strategy: Takes b4 from Black's pieces and prepares b4, but spends a tempo without developing anything or touching the centre. Black takes space.

1.c4 Nf6 2.a4.strategy: Gains a little queenside space but develops nothing and gives up the b4-square for good, where a black knight or bishop can settle. Black takes the centre in the meantime.

1.c4 Nf6 2.b4.name: English Orangutan
1.c4 Nf6 2.b4.strategy: Advances the b-pawn where nothing defends it: after ...e6 or ...e5 the f8-bishop attacks it, and White must spend another tempo saving it or give it up. Development lags while Black takes the centre.

1.c4 Nf6 2.f3.strategy: Prepares e4 but takes f3 from the knight, weakens the e1-h4 diagonal and develops nothing. Black develops freely and takes the centre at once.

1.c4 Nf6 2.f4.name: Bird Opening: Mujannah
1.c4 Nf6 2.f4.strategy: Grabs kingside space and controls e5, but opens the e1-h4 diagonal to the king and develops nothing. Black can simply develop and take the centre.

1.c4 Nf6 2.h3.strategy: Stops ...Ng4 and ...Bg4 but is a slow waiting move that develops nothing. Black takes the centre.

1.c4 Nf6 2.h4.strategy: Spends a tempo on the edge of the board, weakens the g3-square, develops no piece and does nothing for the centre. Black takes space.

1.c4 Nf6 2.c5.strategy: Gains space but moves the same pawn twice and gives up control of d5. The pawn on c5 has no defender: ...e6 or ...e5 opens the f8-bishop against it and ...b6 undermines it, while White has developed nothing.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g4.strategy: Hangs a pawn: 2...Nxg4 wins it at once because nothing defends g4, and h3 only drives the knight to a good square like e5. The kingside is loosened with no lead in development in return.

1.c4 Nf6 2.e4.strategy: Offers the e-pawn: Black simply wins a pawn with 2...Nxe4, and quick development does not regain it, since the knight can retreat to f6 or c5.

1.c4 Nf6.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence
1.c4 Nf6.background: The most common reply to 1.c4; the Encyclopaedia of Chess Openings classifies its independent lines as A15 to A19.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, Hedgehog System
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6.background: The ideas behind the Hedgehog set-up were originally developed in the English Opening, and it first became extensively analysed in the 1970s. Bobby Fischer adopted it with White against Ulf Andersson at Siegen in 1970, one of the first games to feature it, and his crushing win so impressed Andersson that he later became one of the foremost Hedgehog exponents himself.
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6.strategy: Opens the f8-bishop's diagonal and keeps every set-up available: Black can still choose a solid pawn centre, a flexible waiting set-up or an early strike in the centre. White may in turn take space at once. The cost is the c8-bishop, which the e6-pawn shuts in until ...b6 gives it the long diagonal.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e5.strategy: Claims the centre and turns the game into a Reversed Sicilian, a Sicilian with colours swapped and White a tempo ahead. The e5-pawn controls d4, but the d5-square needs watching, since White's c4-pawn and Nc3 both aim at it. A game of classical development, with White setting the pace.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 g6.strategy: Prepares the fianchetto ...Bg7 and quick castling, aiming either to build a pawn centre later or to strike at White's. White can decide which by taking the whole centre with e4, which rules out an immediate ...d5. The cost is central space at first: the g7-bishop only comes alive once Black strikes at the centre with a pawn break.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 d5.name: English Opening: Anglo-Grünfeld Defence
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 d5.background: This independent line of the English Opening generally parallels the development of its 1.d4 counterpart, the Grünfeld Defence, well into the game, hence its name. Ernst Grünfeld introduced that defence into international play at the Bad Pistyan tournament in April 1922.
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 d5.strategy: Strikes at the centre at once and attacks the c4-pawn, so White usually exchanges and Black recaptures with the knight. That gives Black free piece play, at the price of a centralised knight that White can harass with gain of time. White can also avoid the central fight by developing quietly.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 c5.name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 c5.strategy: Controls d4 from the flank, mirroring White's c-pawn, and heads for a manoeuvring game with few early contacts where both sides watch for pawn breaks. The cost is the d5-square, which White's c4-pawn and Nc3 already eye and which a pawn on e4 would control as well.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 Nc6.strategy: Develops with control of d4 and e5 and prepares ...e5, taking space in the centre. The knight blocks the c-pawn, so ...c6 can no longer support ...d5, and a later d5 by White can drive it away again.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, which adds to the f6-knight's pressure on e4. Here the knight on c3 already guards e4, so White can build a broad centre with e4, and Black must undermine it later.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with pawn support while keeping the c8-bishop's diagonal open. White can instead take space at once with e4, and ...d5 then leads to Caro-Kann-like structures in which Black must meet the advance e5 or an exchange on d5.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 d6.strategy: Prepares a central pawn advance or a kingside fianchetto, keeping the structure flexible. The cost is time: White can build a broad pawn centre before Black challenges it.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 b5.strategy: Offers a pawn that both the c4-pawn and the c3-knight attack: after 3.cxb5 White is simply a pawn up, and the half-open b-file is scant compensation.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 a6.strategy: Prepares ...b5 but is too slow: it does nothing for development or the centre, and White takes space unopposed.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 a5.strategy: Gains space on the queenside and covers b4, but weakens b5 and does nothing for development or the centre. White takes the centre with a free hand.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it eyes b4, c5 and c7 but no central square, and blocks the a-pawn. From c6 the same knight would control d4 and e5.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 h6.strategy: Takes g5 from a later Bg5 but costs a tempo, does nothing for the centre or development, and slightly loosens the kingside.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 h5.strategy: Spends a tempo on a flank advance that weakens g5 and g6 and does nothing for the centre or development.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 Ng8.strategy: Returns the knight to its starting square, undoing the previous move. Black has in effect passed twice, so White has two extra tempi for development and the centre.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 Ng4.strategy: Eyes f2 and h2, but both are guarded, and h3 can drive the knight back at any time; Black spends a tempo while White builds the centre.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 Nh5.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it controls f4 and g3 but no central square. White takes the centre, and Be2 or g4 can later drive the knight away with gain of time.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 g5.strategy: Weakens the kingside and does nothing for the centre: after 3.d4 the c1-bishop attacks the unprotected g5-pawn, and guarding it with ...h6 loosens the king's cover further. The f6-knight also blocks the long diagonal of a bishop on g7, so the pawn supports no pressure on d4.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 Rg8.strategy: Gives up the right to castle kingside for good and spends a tempo on a rook move that does nothing for development or the centre.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 Ne4.strategy: Loses the knight outright: 3.Nxe4, and nothing protects e4.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 Nd5.strategy: Hangs the knight to 3.cxd5; the d7-pawn blocks the queen's recapture, so Black has nothing in return.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 e6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 and commits to little else, so Black keeps a solid centre and a flexible pawn structure and decides later how to meet White's set-up. The price is the c8-bishop, which stays shut in behind the e6-pawn for the time being.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6.strategy: Mirrors White's fianchetto and prepares ...Bg7 and short castling, so both sides control the centre from a distance. Black can later occupy it with pawns or challenge it with ...d5. The game stays flexible and tends to be a manoeuvring fight over the centre rather than an early clash.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with a pawn behind it, so that cxd5 can be met by ...cxd5 instead of ...Nxd5, where the knight would stand exposed to Bg2. Black gets a solid pawn structure in which the queen's bishop can still develop before ...e6. The c-pawn is committed, so a later ...c5 costs an extra tempo.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 c5.strategy: Controls d4 and heads for a symmetrical pawn structure, where the fight is over d4 and over queenside expansion with b4 or ...b5. Black accepts that White is a move ahead and has to meet the coming pressure of White's fianchettoed bishop on the long diagonal.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 e5.strategy: Takes the centre at once with a pawn and reaches a reversed Sicilian, in which White has the extra tempo. The game turns on control of d5: White fights for it with the c-pawn, the fianchettoed bishop and the knight, while Black defends the centre with solid development.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 d5.strategy: Strikes at the centre at once, but after 3.cxd5 Nxd5 4.Bg2 the bishop attacks the knight on d5. Black must spend a move saving the knight, so White develops with gain of time; preparing ...d5 first avoids this.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and prepares ...e5 to take space in the centre. It is sound but less flexible than a quieter pawn move: the knight blocks the c-pawn and commits the queen's knight before Black knows White's set-up.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 d6.strategy: Prepares ...e5 and opens the diagonal of the c8-bishop, while a kingside fianchetto stays available. It is sound but modest: the pawn claims less central space than a more direct stand, so White can build up in the centre and keep a small space advantage.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 b6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop to challenge the long diagonal. It is sound, but White can expand in the centre with e4 fairly easily, and Black has less say there than after a more solid pawn move first.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it eyes b4 and c5 but does little for the centre. It needs more moves to become useful, while White gains space in the centre unhindered.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 a6.strategy: Slow, and the ...b5 it prepares fails tactically: once the b-pawn leaves b7, the bishop on g2 hits the rook on a8, so 3.Bg2 b5 4.Bxa8 takes the rook.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 a5.strategy: A slow edge-pawn move that restrains b4 but weakens b5 and does nothing for the centre or for development, while White develops unhindered.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 h6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a rook-pawn move that neither develops a piece nor fights for the centre. White builds a space advantage without hindrance.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 h5.strategy: Heads for ...h4 against g3, but after 3.Nf3 the push ...h4 just drops a pawn to Nxh4, as the g3-pawn guards the knight. The move also weakens g5 and makes kingside castling less attractive while White develops.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 Ng8.strategy: Undoes Black's first move and returns the knight to its starting square, so White has made two useful moves to none and keeps a free hand in the centre.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 Ng4.strategy: Moves the knight a second time without a real threat, since the king guards f2 and the rook guards h2. After 3.h3 it has to move a third time, while White develops unhindered.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 Nh5.strategy: Aims at g3, but the pawn is guarded by f2 and h2, so nothing is threatened. The rim knight can be harassed: 3.e4 opens the queen's diagonal to h5, and White gains time.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 Ne4.strategy: Moves the knight a second time to a square where no pawn supports it: 3.d3 drives it away at once, and White gains time and space while the knight looks for a safe square.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 Rg8.strategy: Spends a tempo and gives up kingside castling for good, since the h8-rook has moved, without helping development or the centre. White simply develops and takes the centre.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 b5.strategy: Gives up a pawn for little: after 3.cxb5 the long diagonal is open, so Bg2 will hit the rook on a8, and Black has to spend time on it instead of on queenside pressure in return for the pawn.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g5.strategy: Weakens f5, h5 and the future king's cover, and the pawn needs support at once: 3.d4 opens the c1-bishop's diagonal against it. The loosened kingside remains a lasting weakness.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 Nd5.strategy: Hangs the knight: the c4-pawn attacks d5 and nothing defends it, as the d7-pawn blocks the queen, so 3.cxd5 wins a piece for nothing.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 c6 3.Nf3.strategy: The flexible developing move: it guards d4 and e5, readies castling and keeps White's central pawn plans open. Against Black's pawn on c6, White aims at a slow game of pressure down the long diagonal rather than an early fight for the centre.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 c6 3.Nf3 d5.strategy: Completes the solid pair of pawns on c6 and d5: the centre square is defended by pawn, knight and queen, and the bishop on c8 stays free to develop outside the pawn chain. Black accepts less space for a robust structure that White's coming fianchetto has to bite on.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 c5 3.Nf3.name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation, Three Knights Variation
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 c5 3.Nf3.strategy: The natural developing move: the knight watches the centre and keeps every plan open, from a fianchetto to a central pawn break. White completes the symmetrical set-up and leaves Black to decide how sharp the game becomes.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 c5 3.g3.name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation, Fianchetto Variation
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 c5 3.g3.strategy: Prepares to bring the bishop to the long diagonal before the knight is committed, so White can wait and see what Black does in the centre. The game stays flexible and manoeuvring: sound and patient, with Black free to choose between a quick central strike and quiet development.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 c5 3.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the knight and adds a second guard of d4, so White cannot easily take the centre with a pawn. The structure stays symmetrical and flexible: a patient game of piece play in which both sides choose their moment to break in the centre.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 c5 3.Nf3 d5.strategy: Strikes at the centre at once and offers to trade the d-pawn for White's c-pawn. Black gets a knight on d5 and easy development; the price is that the symmetry is gone and White has a target to aim at.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 c5 3.Nf3 e5.name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 c5 3.Nf3 e5.strategy: Grabs space with pawns on c5 and e5 that control d4, but fixes the structure: no black pawn can easily challenge a knight on d5 again, so White can settle there and only a piece trade removes it. Playable, but committal.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 c5 3.g3 d5.strategy: Strikes in the centre before White's bishop has even landed, and offers to trade the d-pawn for the c-pawn. Black gets a centralised knight and an easy game, while White aims the bishop and the c3-knight at that knight.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 c5 3.g3 d5 4.cxd5.strategy: Removes the pawn that attacks c4 and prepares to meet the recapture with pressure down the long diagonal. The exchange gives Black a central knight but also a target: once the bishop arrives, d5 is attacked twice.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 c5 3.g3 d5 4.cxd5 Nxd5.strategy: The practically forced recapture: the knight returns to the centre. Black hopes to keep a compact set-up around it, but it will soon be hit by both White's knight and bishop and must decide whether to retreat or to trade.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 c5 3.g3 d5 4.cxd5 Nxd5 5..strategy: Puts the bishop on the long diagonal, where it attacks d5 a second time. The knight is now hit by bishop and knight and guarded only by the queen, so Black has to answer at once and White gains time.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 c5 3.g3 d5 4.cxd5 Nxd5 5..name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation, Rubinstein Variation
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 c5 3.g3 d5 4.cxd5 Nxd5 5..strategy: Steps out of the double attack while still guarding d5, and prepares a wall of pawns on c5 and e5 against White's d-pawn. The retreat costs time, but Black's structure is sound and meets the long-diagonal bishop with a solid centre.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 c5 3.Nf3 d5 4.cxd5.strategy: Settles the tension in the centre at once: White removes the pawn that attacks c4 and, once Black recaptures, can attack the knight on d5 with the knight on c3. The simplest way to a healthy game, trading a flank pawn for a central one.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 c5 3.Nf3 d5 4.cxd5 Nxd5.strategy: Recaptures with the knight, which develops and in turn attacks the knight on c3. The piece is centralised but also a target, so White can challenge it at once; Black accepts that for easy development and a firm hold on the centre.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 c5 3.Nf3 d5 4.cxd5 Nxd5 5.strategy: Opens the f1-bishop and prepares to challenge the centre with a pawn push on d4. It shuts in the c1-bishop for now and does not rush at the d5 knight: White wants a solid game and a pawn break later.

Prepares to fianchetto the bishop but gives up the fight for the centre: Black keeps the strong knight on d5 and the larger share of space. White must rely on long-diagonal pressure and slow manoeuvring, which is sound but the passive way to treat the position.

Develops a piece and adds a second guard of d4, so White cannot easily challenge the centre with a pawn. Black enjoys the extra space White has allowed, at the price of a slower game in which the d5 knight can come under pressure.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 c5 3.Nf3 d5 4.cxd5 Nxd5 5.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 c5 3.Nf3 d5 4.cxd5 Nxd5 5.strategy: Supports the knight on d5 with a pawn and opens the diagonal of the f8-bishop. The c8-bishop is shut in for the time being, so Black aims for a compact, solid game and relies on piece play rather than space.
Completes the kingside fianchetto and prepares to castle. White's own knight on f3 still stands in the bishop's way, so for the moment only the c3-knight presses on d5, and White is content to wait.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 c5 3.Nf3 d5 4.cxd5 Nxd5 5.name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation, Rubinstein Variation
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 c5 3.Nf3 d5 4.cxd5 Nxd5 5.strategy: The retreat that defines this set-up: the knight leaves d5 before a trade could pull the queen onto the long diagonal. From c7 it still guards d5 and makes room for a solid wall of pawns on c5 and e5 that holds down d4. The price is time.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 d5 3.cxd5.strategy: Settles the centre at once: White trades the c-pawn for Black's central pawn and, after the recapture, can attack the knight on d5 with the c3-knight. The simplest way to a normal game, with the initiative in White's hands.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 d5 3.cxd5 Nxd5.strategy: The natural recapture: the knight reaches the centre, develops and attacks the knight on c3. Black enjoys central space and easy development, but the knight is exposed and White can start working against it at once.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 d5 3.cxd5 Nxd5 4.g3.strategy: The calm way to treat the position: White fianchettoes the bishop and builds no central pawns for Black to attack. It aims the bishop at the knight on d5 and trades some sharpness for a safe, flexible game.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 d5 3.cxd5 Nxd5 4.Nf3.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, Anglo-Grünfeld Variation
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 d5 3.cxd5 Nxd5 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops and keeps every plan open; a central pawn advance is a real option, so the knight on d5 cannot count on staying put. White decides little yet and Black decides what kind of game it becomes.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 d5 3.cxd5 Nxd5 4.g3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the bishop so that it bears down on the long diagonal and on c3. Black gets a compact, flexible position without weaknesses, and a bishop that pressures White's centre from a distance.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 d5 3.cxd5 Nxd5 4.Nf3 g6.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, Anglo-Grünfeld Variation
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 d5 3.cxd5 Nxd5 4.Nf3 g6.strategy: Prepares the kingside fianchetto, so that the bishop will watch the long diagonal and the c3-knight. Black keeps a compact structure and a flexible, counter-punching game against whatever centre White builds.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 d5 3.cxd5 Nxd5 4.Nf3 c5.strategy: Challenges the centre with a flank pawn and steers into the symmetrical structure by transposition, with the knight already on d5 and White to move. Black chooses a more classical fight in place of a fianchetto set-up.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 d5 3.cxd5 Nxd5 4.g3 g6 5..strategy: Develops with gain of time: d5 is now attacked by bishop and knight and guarded only by the queen, so Black has to answer at once. White wins the opening skirmish for the long diagonal.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 d5 3.cxd5 Nxd5 4.g3 g6 5..name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, Anglo-Grünfeld Variation
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 d5 3.cxd5 Nxd5 4.g3 g6 5..strategy: Retreats and keeps the pieces on, avoiding an exchange that would hand White a pawn on c3 and an open b-file. Black keeps a compact position and the plan of the fianchetto, at the cost of time and a less active knight.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 d5 3.cxd5 Nxd5 4.g3 g6 5..name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, Anglo-Grünfeld Variation
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 d5 3.cxd5 Nxd5 4.g3 g6 5..strategy: Trades off the attacked knight, so White normally recaptures with the b-pawn. Black spends no time on a retreat and can put the bishop on g7 against the new pawn on c3; White gets a broad pawn centre and an open b-file to work with.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 d5 3.cxd5 Nxd5 4.Nf3 g6 5.strategy: Matches Black's plan with a fianchetto of White's own: the bishop will take the long diagonal, and the knight on f3 stays flexible for now. A quiet, positional game follows in which both sides keep their central pawns back.

Completes the fianchetto: the bishop attacks the knight on c3 along the long diagonal and adds to the pressure on the centre. Black will castle soon and plays for a game of long-range pieces with a sound king.

Completes White's own fianchetto and prepares to castle, so the two fianchettoed bishops now face each other across the board. White's knight on f3 stands in front of the bishop for now, which keeps the pressure on d5 modest.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 d5 3.cxd5 Nxd5 4.Nf3 g6 5.name: English Opening: Anglo-Grünfeld Defence, Korchnoi Variation
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 d5 3.cxd5 Nxd5 4.Nf3 g6 5.strategy: A direct claim to the centre: the pawn denies White's knight the e5 square and is backed by the bishop on g7. The knight on d5 is guarded only by the queen, so White can trade it, and Black must be ready to recapture with the queen.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the kingside knight and keeps every option open: it guards d4 and e5, so a challenge to the centre meets a ready defender. White has not yet decided between an early central advance and a slower build-up, and Black is free to choose its own set-up in return.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.e4.name: English Opening: Mikenas-Carls Variation
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.e4.background: Also called the Flohr–Mikenas–Carls Variation, after Salo Flohr, Vladas Mikėnas and Carl Johan Margot Carls.
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.e4.strategy: Grabs the centre at once and threatens to drive the f6-knight away with e5. White gives up the quiet flexibility of the knight development for space, betting that pawns on c4 and e4 plus the c3-knight hold the centre while Black, with no pawn in the middle yet, has to react accurately.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.e4 d5.strategy: The principal answer: Black strikes at the centre immediately, and the pawn attacks both c4 and e4. The price is that the f6-knight stays exposed to an advance of White's e-pawn, so the game turns sharp at once and Black has to be accurate.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.e4 Nc6.name: English Opening: Mikenas-Carls Variation
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.e4 Nc6.background: Known as the Kevitz Variation, after Alexander Kevitz.
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.e4 Nc6.strategy: Pressures the centre with a piece instead of a pawn: the knight eyes d4 and e5, so an advance of the e-pawn simply loses it to a capture. Black commits a piece before the structure is clear and blocks the c-pawn, and White keeps the extra space.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.e4 c5.name: English Opening: Mikenas-Carls, Sicilian
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.e4 c5.strategy: Challenges the centre from the side: the pawn takes d4 away from White, so White cannot build a broad pawn centre without a fight, and Black heads for an unbalanced structure. The cost is time, since White gains space with tempo against the f6-knight before Black has developed much.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.Nf3 c5.strategy: Stakes a claim to d4 with a pawn and heads for a symmetrical fight in which both sides contest d4 and d5. The play turns tactical, and Black keeps the freedom to choose the structure later.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.Nf3 b6.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, Queen's Indian Formation
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.Nf3 b6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop, which will press on the long diagonal towards e4 and the centre from a distance instead of occupying it with pawns. It is a solid set-up, at the price of a slower fight for the centre.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, Nimzo-English
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4.strategy: Attacks the c3-knight, which guards both d5 and e4, and threatens to take it and double White's pawns. If Black takes, White gets the bishop pair in return for the damaged structure; Black gets quick development and a firm grip on the centre squares.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.e4 c5 4.e5.strategy: Gains space and attacks the knight in one move, before Black has developed another piece. The pawn is advanced and for the moment defended by nothing, so White must support it soon, but the lead in space is real and Black has to spend time on the retreat.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.e4 c5 4.e5 Ng8.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, Flohr-Mikenas-Carls Variation, Nei Gambit
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.e4 c5 4.e5 Ng8.strategy: The knight goes back to its home square: Black loses time and falls behind in development, but the pawn structure stays intact and White's e5 pawn has to be defended. Black plays to undermine that pawn and win back the time with pressure on the centre.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.e4 d5 4.e5.name: English Opening: Mikenas-Carls Variation
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.e4 d5 4.e5.background: The most common continuation of the Mikėnas–Carls Variation is 3...d5 4.e5, known as the Flohr Variation.
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.e4 d5 4.e5.strategy: Takes space and hits the knight with tempo, but Black hits back by attacking the c3-knight. Usually a run of exchanges follows that leaves White with doubled c-pawns and Black's queen active on f6 with pressure on c3; the game is open, and each side must know the forcing play.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.e4.strategy: Seizes the centre with pawns before the bishop can organise its pressure from b7. White gains space, but the pawn on e4 becomes the target of Black's pieces, so it needs support at once and White accepts a game of defending a strong centre.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.e4 Bb7.strategy: Puts the bishop on its diagonal at once, where it joins the f6-knight in attacking e4. The pawn is attacked twice and defended once, so White must reinforce it, and Black's whole set-up is aimed at that centre pawn.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.e4 Bb7 5.Bd.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, Queen's Indian Variation
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.e4 Bb7 5.Bd.strategy: Defends the e4 pawn a second time with a developing move and prepares castling. White keeps its strong pawn pair on c4 and e4, and the game becomes a test of whether that centre is a strength or a target for Black's pawn levers.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4 4.g4.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, Zvjaginsev-Krasenkow Attack
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4 4.g4.strategy: An aggressive pawn lunge: White grabs kingside space and threatens to chase the f6-knight away, but it loosens its own king before castling and the pawn can be taken. White must justify it with activity and a lead in development, so it is a risky, offbeat choice.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 g6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight and leaves the pawn decision for later: White controls d4 and e5 and can still choose between a flexible English set-up and opening the centre. Black has declared a kingside fianchetto, and White does not commit itself against it yet.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop will press along the long diagonal against the c3-knight and d4 once the f6-knight steps aside. Black gets a safe king after castling and a flexible set-up that waits for White to reveal its centre.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.e4.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, Anti-Anti-Grünfeld
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.e4.strategy: Claims the centre with pawns on c4 and e4, so d5 is controlled three times and Black cannot free its game easily. White gains space and aims for a middlegame in which Black must undermine the big centre with its pieces and pawn breaks.
